row.title: The Girl Who Owned a Bear
row.author: L Frank Baum

plot_extraction.response_text:
Left alone while her mother shops and the maid works, Jane Gladys receives a strange book from a disgruntled salesman seeking revenge because her father had thrown him out of his office. When she opens the book, its illustrated characters spring to life: a clown with no back, a talking monkey, a lopsided donkey, a toothless leopard, and finally a dangerous grizzly bear.

The bear announces that, according to the book, he must eat little girls. As he approaches, Jane Gladys thinks quickly and argues that because the book was given to her and bears her name, she owns everything in it—including the bear—so he cannot eat his owner. The clown confirms her claim, and the bear reluctantly relents. When the doorbell signals her mother’s return, all the characters rush back into the book, leaving Jane Gladys safe.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a clear, linear, third-person narrative style shaped for children, combining domestic realism with whimsical fantasy. It begins in a secure, recognisable household setting and introduces the supernatural gradually: first through the suspicious book agent, then through a succession of illustrations that spring from the pages. The narrator remains close to Jane Gladys’s experience while retaining an external, lightly omniscient perspective, occasionally addressing the reader directly with phrases such as “Perhaps you can imagine.” This creates the manner of an adult storyteller speaking warmly and confidently to a young audience.

The diction is simple, concrete and slightly old-fashioned. Expressions such as “down-town,” “papa,” “mamma,” “vest pocket” and “good-by,” along with the child’s pronunciation of “immediately” as “‘meejitly,” give the prose a period flavour. Descriptions are economical but visually vivid, relying on easily pictured details, strong colours and familiar objects. Characters are established through a few conspicuous physical traits: the visitor is short, fat, bald and shabby; the clown is brightly coloured but blank at the back; and the animals possess obvious defects inherited from their illustrations. The language avoids lyrical complexity in favour of accessibility, momentum and comic clarity.

Sentence structure is generally straightforward, with short declarative sentences used for action and longer compound or complex sentences used to explain circumstances. Temporal markers such as “Soon,” “Then,” “Just then” and “But before” keep the sequence easy to follow. Repetition provides rhythm and reinforces the fairy-tale logic: Jane Gladys turns a page, a figure emerges, and its visual defect becomes the subject of complaint. Exclamation marks, abrupt interjections and emphatic phrasing animate moments of surprise, indignation and danger without making them psychologically intense.

Dialogue dominates much of the story and performs several functions at once: it characterises the speakers, explains the fantasy’s rules and sustains the comedy. Jane Gladys speaks with childish directness but also with dignity, practicality and moral certainty. The book agent’s exaggerated politeness and mock-vindictive reasoning make him comically sinister rather than genuinely terrifying. The clown and animals speak like irritable adults, complaining about artistic perspective, anatomy, authorship and representation. Their formal or argumentative speech contrasts humorously with their absurd condition. Exchanges are brisk, often structured as question and answer, and regularly end in a comic reversal or literal-minded retort.

The prevailing tone is playful, mischievous and gently suspenseful. Threats are presented seriously enough to create tension, but absurdity continually undercuts fear. The leopard looks ferocious but has neither teeth nor claws; the donkey cannot stand properly because its legs were drawn out of perspective; the clown has no back because only his front was illustrated. Even the bear’s intention to eat the heroine is governed by what the author has written about him. Violence therefore remains hypothetical and cartoon-like, appropriate to a children’s comic fantasy.

A notable stylistic feature is the story’s metafictional humour. The creatures understand themselves as products of a book and blame the artist and author for their bodies, personalities and appetites. The physical conventions of flat illustration become literal limitations when the figures enter three-dimensional space. This produces an imaginative but logically consistent conceit: whatever was omitted, distorted or prescribed on the page continues to control the living figure. The story repeatedly exploits the gap between representation and reality.

The plot follows an accumulative structure. A calm domestic opening gives way to the enigmatic gift, after which each turned page introduces a new and slightly more disruptive figure. The clown, monkey, donkey and leopard chiefly increase comic disorder, while the bear introduces the central danger and forms the climax. Jane Gladys resolves the threat not through force or rescue but through quick reasoning: because she owns the book, she owns the bear. The ringing doorbell restores ordinary domestic order, and the creatures retreat into the book in a rapid burst of sound and movement.

Characterisation is broad and functional, resembling fairy-tale or comic archetypes rather than psychological realism. Jane Gladys is innocent but self-possessed, loyal to her father and capable of thinking under pressure. The fantastic figures are defined by one visual flaw and one dominant attitude, usually vanity, grievance or foolishness. The narrative repeatedly places the sensible child against irrational or pompous adults and creatures, allowing youthful common sense to triumph over pretension and brute force.

The ending adds an explicit moral in the manner of traditional children’s literature. Rather than leaving the lesson implicit, the narrator states that the episode teaches the value of thinking “quickly and clearly upon all occasions.” This coda is didactic but remains humorous because it treats the fantastic danger as if it were a practical example from everyday life. Overall, the style blends accessible storytelling, cumulative fantasy, verbal comedy, mild peril and overt moral instruction, with a strong emphasis on literal logic and the playful exposure of how books and pictures construct fictional reality.

# Jane Gladys and the Picture Book

Jane Gladys was eight years old and lived in a tall brick house with green shutters. Her papa had gone down-town directly after breakfast, as he always did, and her mamma had gone shopping for a new bonnet. The maid was in the kitchen polishing the silver spoons and singing so loudly that she could not have heard a lion sneeze in the parlor.

Therefore Jane Gladys was alone.

She did not mind this. She sat upon the red carpet with her dolls arranged before her and was teaching them how to behave at a tea-party.

“No, Arabella,” she said severely, “you must not put your feet upon the table. If you do it again, you shall go to bed ’meejitly.”

Just then the doorbell rang.

The maid continued to sing in the kitchen, so Jane Gladys went to the door herself. Upon the step stood a short, fat man with a bald head, a shabby coat and a black leather case under his arm. His necktie was yellow, his shoes were dusty, and he smiled as if smiling were disagreeable work.

“Is Mr. Gladys at home?” he asked.

“No,” replied Jane Gladys. “Papa is down-town.”

“Ah!” said the man. “That is fortunate—I mean, that is unfortunate. And your mamma?”

“She is buying a bonnet.”

“Even more fortunate! That is, of course, even more unfortunate.”

He opened his leather case and took out a large book bound in purple cloth. A silver star was stamped upon the cover, and beneath the star were printed the words:

**WONDERFUL CREATURES OF EVERY LAND**

“I have brought your papa a present,” said the man.

“Why?”

The visitor rubbed his bald head.

“Because yesterday I called at his office to sell him twelve books concerning the habits of successful men. Your papa said he was busy and ordered me to leave.”

“Papa is very busy,” explained Jane Gladys.

“He also told a clerk to put me out.”

“Then perhaps you would not go.”

“I had not finished my speech,” said the man indignantly. “No gentleman should throw out a book agent before the end of his speech. So I have come to reward him.”

Jane Gladys looked doubtfully at the purple book.

“It does not sound like a reward.”

“You are a thoughtful child,” said the man. “What is your name?”

“Jane Gladys.”

Taking a pencil from his vest pocket, he wrote upon the first page:

**For Jane Gladys, with the respectful compliments of a friend of her papa.**

“There!” he said. “Now the book belongs to you. Open it whenever you grow tired of dolls. You will find the pictures unusually lifelike.”

“Thank you,” said Jane Gladys, for she had been taught to be polite even to unpleasant persons.

The short man bowed until his bald head nearly struck the door.

“Give my kindest regards to your papa,” he said, “and tell him I hope the book will amuse the entire household.”

Then he hurried down the steps, chuckling in a manner that was not at all respectful.

Jane Gladys carried the book into the parlor. It was heavy, and something inside it seemed to rustle, although the windows were closed.

She placed it on the carpet.

“I shall look at only one picture,” she told her dolls. “Then we will continue the tea-party.”

The book opened easily. On the first page was a coloured picture of a clown. He wore a red coat spotted with blue moons, yellow trousers, green slippers and a tall white cap. His cheeks were round, his mouth was wide, and he had been painted entirely from the front.

“That is a very bright clown,” said Jane Gladys.

The clown winked.

Jane Gladys leaned nearer. The clown placed both hands against the edge of the picture, pulled himself out of the page and tumbled headfirst upon the carpet.

“Dear me!” he cried, sitting up. “What a narrow house!”

“It is not a house,” said Jane Gladys. “It is a book.”

“Then I dislike books. Kindly assist me.”

She helped him stand. When he turned around, Jane Gladys gave a little gasp. The clown had a face, chest, arms and legs, but he had no back at all. Behind him there was only a flat white surface.

“You are not finished,” she said.

“I am perfectly aware of it!” snapped the clown. “The stupid artist drew my front and neglected the remainder. How am I to sit comfortably? How am I to lean against a wall? I cannot even turn my back upon an enemy.”

“You might walk backward.”

“And spend my life looking where I have been instead of where I am going? What a ridiculous suggestion!”

The clown examined the parlor and then bowed to the dolls.

“Ladies,” he said, “I apologize for my incomplete appearance.”

Jane Gladys turned another page.

This picture showed a brown monkey sitting in a tree. He wore a little red waistcoat and held a coconut in one hand. The instant the page lay flat, the monkey sprang into the room, landed upon the table and knocked over the dolls’ teapot.

“Mind the china!” cried Jane Gladys.

“Mind the artist!” answered the monkey. “He has given me two left hands.”

He held them up, and this was true. Both thumbs pointed the same way.

“That must be inconvenient,” said Jane Gladys.

“Inconvenient? It is a catastrophe! I cannot button my waistcoat. I cannot peel my coconut properly. I cannot shake hands without first explaining which hand I mean.”

“You might ask the clown to help you.”

“He has no back,” said the monkey.

“That is no reason I cannot button waistcoats,” declared the clown. “Come here.”

They began pulling at the buttons, each giving directions to the other and neither accomplishing anything. While they quarrelled, Jane Gladys turned the next page.

A gray donkey stood in a meadow. His head was too large, one ear was short, the other ear was long, and his four legs pointed in four different directions.

“Poor thing,” said Jane Gladys.

At once the donkey slid out of the picture and fell sideways upon the rug.

“I object to being pitied,” he announced.

Jane Gladys and the clown tried to set him upright, but whenever two of his legs touched the floor, the others waved helplessly in the air.

“The artist did not understand perspective,” complained the donkey. “He drew my front legs as if they were far away and my hind legs as if they belonged to another donkey.”

“Can you walk?” asked Jane Gladys.

“Certainly. I can walk north, south, east and west at the same time.”

“That must save trouble.”

“It causes trouble!” cried the donkey. “Whenever I intend to go forward, three-quarters of me prefer another direction.”

He attempted a step. His front half moved toward the piano, his hind half moved toward the door, and the rest of him sat down with a thump.

The monkey laughed so hard that he dropped his coconut upon the clown’s toe.

“Ow!” shouted the clown.

“Pray excuse me,” said the monkey. “With two left hands one cannot be expected to drop things correctly.”

Jane Gladys was beginning to think the book agent’s gift more troublesome than amusing. She decided to shut the volume, but as she reached for the cover, the pages fluttered by themselves and stopped at a picture of a spotted leopard.

The leopard’s eyes were yellow. His body crouched close to the ground, his tail curled behind him, and his mouth was open in a terrible snarl.

“Oh!” said Jane Gladys.

The leopard leaped from the book.

The clown jumped behind the sofa, although he could not properly turn his back while doing so. The monkey scrambled up the curtains. The donkey tried to run in four directions and remained exactly where he was.

The leopard landed before Jane Gladys and roared.

It was not a very successful roar. It sounded like wind passing through an empty cupboard.

“Are you going to bite me?” Jane Gladys asked.

“I should be delighted,” said the leopard gloomily, “but the artist forgot my teeth.”

He opened his mouth wider. There were no teeth inside.

“Then you cannot hurt me.”

“I have claws,” said the leopard.

He lifted one paw and looked at it. Then he lifted another.

“No, I have not,” he added bitterly. “The careless fellow painted round yellow toes. How can a leopard maintain his reputation with round yellow toes?”

“You still look fierce,” said Jane Gladys, wishing to comfort him.

“Looking fierce is useful only while one remains in a picture. Out here, people ask one to prove it.”

The monkey came down from the curtains.

“You might frighten mice,” he suggested.

“I am a leopard, not a house cat!”

“You are badly drawn, whatever you are,” said the clown.

This remark began a noisy argument. The leopard insisted that spots were more artistic than blue moons. The clown replied that a proper coat was superior to any quantity of fur. The monkey declared that neither of them possessed useful hands. The donkey, still lying on his side, said that hands were an unnecessary luxury.

Jane Gladys clapped her own hands.

“Be quiet!” she commanded. “Mamma will return soon, and she will not like finding wild animals in the parlor.”

The creatures became silent.

“You must all go back into the book,” she continued.

“Never!” cried the clown. “It is flat in there.”

“There are no buttons on the trees,” said the monkey.

“The meadow slopes the wrong way,” groaned the donkey.

“And everyone expects me to be savage,” said the leopard.

“But this is my house,” said Jane Gladys.

Before anyone could answer, the pages began to flutter again.

They turned slowly at first, then faster and faster, until they stopped upon a dark picture of a forest. Between two black pine trees stood a great grizzly bear.

He was twice as tall as Jane Gladys and four times as broad. His fur was thick, his claws were long, and, unlike the leopard, he had a splendid set of white teeth.

The clown hid behind the curtain. The monkey hid behind the clown. The leopard crawled under the table, and the donkey shut his eyes.

The bear stepped out of the book.

The carpet shook beneath him.

“Good afternoon,” he said in a deep voice.

“Good afternoon,” replied Jane Gladys, because politeness is useful even when speaking to bears.

The bear sniffed the air.

“I smell a little girl.”

“That is probably me.”

“Are you Jane Gladys?”

“Yes.”

“Then everything is in order.”

“What order?”

The bear pointed one long claw at the printed words beneath his picture.

Jane Gladys read them aloud:

“‘The grizzly bear is the most dreadful of all the creatures in this volume. Upon leaving the forest, he will at once eat any little girl he finds.’”

“There,” said the bear. “You see my duty.”

“I do not think it is your duty,” answered Jane Gladys.

“It is printed in black ink.”

“Printing a wicked thing does not make it right.”

“That may be so outside books,” replied the bear, “but I am a book bear. I must follow what the author wrote.”

He moved one step nearer.

Perhaps you can imagine how Jane Gladys felt. The clown had no back, the monkey had two left hands, the donkey could not stand, and the leopard possessed neither teeth nor claws. Not one of them could protect her.

Still, Jane Gladys did not scream. Screaming might have pleased the bear, and it certainly would not have improved matters.

Instead she looked at the book.

“Wait,” she said.

The bear stopped.

“Why?”

“I wish to read something.”

“Be quick. I have been waiting in that forest for years.”

Jane Gladys turned to the first page and pointed to the words written by the book agent.

“What does this say?”

The clown peeped from behind the curtain.

“‘For Jane Gladys,’” he read, “‘with the respectful compliments of a friend of her papa.’”

“So the book was given to me,” said Jane Gladys.

“Plainly,” agreed the monkey.

“And if the book was given to me, it belongs to me.”

“I see no error in that,” said the leopard.

“Everything in the book belongs to me also—the pictures, the trees, the coconut, the meadow and the creatures.”

The bear frowned.

“That is a troublesome argument.”

“It is a correct argument,” said Jane Gladys. “You came out of my book. Therefore you are my bear.”

The clown stepped boldly into view.

“She owns every coloured inch of you,” he declared. “I am a person of no back, but I understand property.”

“You cannot eat your owner,” continued Jane Gladys. “An owner may feed her bear, brush her bear or order her bear back into his picture. But if a bear eats his owner, then he has no owner, and a creature belonging to a book cannot belong to nobody.”

The bear scratched his head.

“The author said I must eat little girls.”

“He did not say you must eat your owner.”

“No,” admitted the bear.

“And my name is written before your picture. That rule came first.”

The monkey nodded eagerly.

“Words printed at the front of a book are always more important. Otherwise they would be printed at the back.”

“That is not always true,” said the clown, “but it sounds convincing.”

The bear sat down heavily.

“I dislike clever little girls,” he grumbled. “Authors ought not put them into dangerous situations. They spoil everything.”

“I am glad to spoil this,” said Jane Gladys.

At that moment the front doorbell rang.

“Mamma!” cried Jane Gladys.

At once the parlor was filled with confusion.

“The book!” shouted the clown.

He dived toward it and slipped between the pages like a coloured card. The monkey followed, carrying his coconut in both left hands. The donkey rolled across the carpet, struck the book with his nose and vanished into his crooked meadow. The leopard sprang after him, pausing only to give one last toothless snarl.

The bear rose.

“May I eat the maid?” he asked hopefully.

“No.”

“The book agent?”

“No.”

“Anyone at all?”

“No. Go back to your forest ’meejitly.”

The bear sighed, climbed onto the open page and became flat and still between the pine trees. Jane Gladys slammed the cover just as the maid hurried from the kitchen to answer the door.

Mamma entered carrying three parcels and wearing her old bonnet.

“Did you have a pleasant afternoon, dear?” she asked.

“Very interesting,” said Jane Gladys.

“And what is that large purple book?”

“A present from a friend of papa.”

That evening Papa examined the volume. He looked at the inscription, frowned, and locked the book in the top drawer of his desk.

“The man who brought this is no friend of mine,” he said.

“I thought perhaps he was not,” replied Jane Gladys.

She never opened the book again, although she sometimes heard muffled complaints from inside the drawer. The clown wanted a back, the monkey wanted a proper right hand, the donkey wanted four sensible legs, and the leopard wanted teeth. The bear merely growled.

Thus Jane Gladys learned—and it is well for all of us to remember—that when danger steps out of a book or enters by an ordinary door, the best thing to do is to think quickly and clearly. A small person with a sound argument may sometimes defeat even a very large bear.

Every morning at seven, the sea left a letter on Mara Vale’s doorstep.

The first arrived in October, folded into a square and sealed with gray wax. It was damp but not soaked, though the tide had climbed the harbor wall during the night and flooded half of Lantern Street. Her name was written across the front in a narrow, slanting hand:

**MARA VALE, CLOCK REPAIRER**

Inside was a single sentence.

**Your brother is alive beneath the western bell.**

Mara read it twice, then carried it to the stove and held one corner over the flame. The paper browned. The ink remained black. Before the fire could take it, she dropped the letter into the sink and turned away.

Her brother, Eli, had been dead for eleven years.

The western bell had not rung for twelve.

In Bellweather, these facts were as solid as the cliffs.

The town stood on a crescent of black rock at the edge of a cold northern sea. Five bell towers watched over it—north, south, east, west, and center—built generations ago to warn of storms. Four still rang. The western tower had been silent since the night Eli Vale disappeared.

People said the rope had snapped. Mara knew better. She had been there.

At seven the next morning, the sea left another letter.

**You have forgotten what you promised him.**

Mara tore it in half.

On the third morning:

**Ask Tomas Reed who cut the rope.**

That one she did not burn.

Tomas Reed kept the town records in the lower rooms of the council hall. He had been old when Mara was a child and seemed to have aged only in texture since then, like leather left in sunlight. He wore three pairs of spectacles on cords around his neck and trusted none of them.

When Mara entered his office, he was standing on a stool, arguing with a shelf.

“You moved,” he told it.

The shelf said nothing.

“Tomas.”

He climbed down carefully. “Mara Vale. If this concerns the clock in the council chamber, it loses seven minutes a day because the mayor insists on winding it backward.”

“It concerns the western bell.”

Tomas became still.

Mara placed the letter on his desk. His eyes moved over the sentence. Then he removed one pair of spectacles and put on another.

“Where did you get this?”

“It was on my doorstep.”

“Who delivered it?”

“The sea, according to local gossip.”

“Local gossip has poor handwriting.”

“Did you cut the rope?”

Tomas looked toward the window. Beyond the warped glass, gulls wheeled above the wet roofs.

“At your age,” he said, “you should know that questions are rarely dangerous. Answers are.”

“Did you cut it?”

“No.”

“Who did?”

“Your brother.”

Mara stared at him.

Tomas lowered himself into his chair. “Sit down.”

“I prefer standing.”

“You always did.”

He opened a drawer and removed a ledger bound in cracked blue cloth. Its pages smelled of salt and dust. He turned to a date eleven years earlier: the seventeenth of November.

Mara remembered the date without needing to see it. She remembered the storm pressing its enormous hands against the windows. She remembered fifteen-year-old Eli grinning beneath a yellow oilskin, daring her to follow him up the western tower. She remembered the iron steps, wet beneath her boots, and the black bell hanging overhead.

Most of all, she remembered the thing they had heard inside it.

Not a ring.

A voice.

“Mara,” Eli had whispered, “it knows my name.”

She had laughed because she was afraid.

In Tomas’s ledger, the entries for that night were sparse.

**9:14 p.m. — Western bell sounded without human action.**

**9:20 p.m. — Tower keeper ordered evacuation.**

**9:26 p.m. — Bell rope severed.**

**9:31 p.m. — One child missing.**

Child. As if Eli had been any child. As if he had not collected sea glass in blue jars, whistled through the gap in his front teeth, and slept with one foot outside his blankets even in winter.

“You wrote that the rope was severed,” Mara said.

“I wrote what I was told.”

“By whom?”

“By you.”

The room seemed to tilt.

“That isn’t true.”

Tomas opened another drawer and took out a small brass key.

“You came to me before dawn,” he said. “Your hands were bleeding. You gave me this and told me to hide it until the sea began writing.”

Mara did not touch the key.

“I never did that.”

“You did.”

“I would remember.”

“Would you?”

He spoke gently, which angered her more than cruelty might have.

Mara snatched up the key. “What does it open?”

“The door beneath the western bell.”

“There is no door beneath the western bell.”

Tomas replaced the spectacles around his neck one pair at a time.

“You said that too.”

At seven the following morning, the fourth letter waited on her doorstep.

**Bring the clock that has never worked. Come before the lowest tide.**

Mara owned two hundred and six clocks.

They crowded the walls of her shop, stood in glass cabinets, and lay in careful pieces across her workbenches. There were walnut mantel clocks, brass carriage clocks, silver pocket watches, cuckoo clocks with painted doors, and one complicated French clock whose moon turned through a sky of blue enamel.

At six every evening, Mara wound them all.

At midnight, the shop became a forest of ticking.

Only one clock had never worked.

It had belonged to Eli.

He had built it from scraps when he was thirteen: a crooked wooden box containing mismatched gears, a bent spring, and a white face on which he had painted thirteen numbers. The thirteenth sat where twelve should have been, at the top.

“What hour is that?” Mara had asked when he showed it to her.

“The hour that gets lost,” he said.

Now she took it from the highest shelf. Dust softened its edges. On the back, beneath a stain she had always assumed was rust, someone had scratched three words:

**TURN BACK TIDE.**

Mara closed the shop early.

The lowest tide came just after dusk. It drew the sea away from the western cliffs, exposing rocks that shone like the backs of sleeping animals. The western bell tower stood at the edge of the town, fenced and abandoned, its stones furred with salt.

Mara found the gate unlocked.

Inside, the air smelled of iron. The staircase curled upward into darkness, but she did not climb. She searched the circular room at ground level, pressing the brass key against cracks, hinges, and gaps between stones.

At last she noticed a keyhole hidden behind a loose piece of mortar.

The key turned.

A section of wall opened inward.

Beyond it, steps descended beneath the tower.

Mara carried Eli’s clock in one hand and a lantern in the other. The stairs were narrow and slick. They went down farther than the base of the cliff, farther than seemed possible. The sound of the sea grew louder, not above her but around her, as though she were descending into the throat of some vast creature.

At the bottom stood a red door.

A brass plate at its center had been engraved with a single word:

**LATE**

Mara placed her palm against the wood. It was warm.

The door opened before she could knock.

On the other side was Bellweather.

Yet it was not the Bellweather she knew.

The town lay under a clear summer sky. Sunlight filled the streets. Boats with bright sails crowded the harbor, and the five towers rang together in a joyful storm of bronze.

People moved through the square, but none had faces.

Where eyes and mouths should have been, their features blurred like reflections troubled by rain.

All except one.

Eli stood beside the fountain.

He was fifteen.

His yellow oilskin was unbuttoned. His dark hair fell across his forehead, and the gap still showed between his front teeth.

“You took your time,” he said.

Mara could not move.

He came toward her, then stopped a few feet away. His smile faded.

“You got old.”

“You didn’t.”

“I was busy.”

She set the lantern down because her hand had begun to shake. “Are you alive?”

“Sometimes.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means you’ll need a better question.”

Mara crossed the distance between them and struck him across the face.

Her palm met warm skin.

Eli touched his cheek. “I suppose I deserved that.”

She struck him again, then seized his coat and pulled him into her arms. He felt real. He smelled of rain, wet wool, and the peppermint sweets he used to steal from their mother’s pantry.

Mara held him until grief became anger again.

“You left me.”

“No,” he said against her shoulder. “You left me.”

She pushed him away.

The faceless people had stopped walking. Every blank head turned toward them.

Eli took Mara’s hand. “We can’t stay in the open.”

He led her through streets that were familiar and wrong. The baker’s shop sold loaves shaped like fish. The council hall had no doors. Mara’s own clock shop stood on the corner, though it had not existed when Eli disappeared. Through its windows she saw herself at many ages—eight, seventeen, thirty, forty—bending over clocks that ran backward.

They entered a small house behind the eastern tower. Inside, hundreds of bells hung from the ceiling. None moved, yet their tones trembled in the air.

“What is this place?” Mara asked.

“The hour that gets lost.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It’s the only one I have.” Eli sat at a table. “Every clock loses something, Mara. A second here, a minute there. People think the lost time vanishes. It doesn’t. It washes down to this place.”

She looked out the window. The sun had not shifted.

“The night you disappeared—”

“The bell opened the way. It had done so before. That’s why the towers were built. Not to warn the town about storms. To drown out the voices beneath the sea.”

Mara remembered the sound inside the western bell calling Eli’s name.

“You cut the rope,” she said.

“I tried to stop it ringing. But it was too late. The door opened.”

“And you went through.”

“We both did.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

He reached across the table and touched a pale scar on her wrist. Mara had carried it for eleven years without remembering how she got it.

“You held on to me,” Eli said. “The tide was pulling us deeper. The people here came for us. So you made a bargain.”

“I don’t remember.”

“That was the price.”

A bell near the ceiling gave a small, clear note.

Outside, the faceless townspeople gathered around the house.

“What bargain?”

Eli looked at the broken clock in her arms.

“You asked the hour to take your memory instead of your life. You promised to build a clock that could return what had been lost. Then you escaped and sealed the door.”

“Why didn’t you come with me?”

His expression answered before he spoke.

“The door needed someone on this side.”

Mara stood so abruptly that the hanging bells trembled.

“No. I wouldn’t have agreed to that.”

“You were sixteen. We were drowning. I told you to go.”

“And I obeyed?”

“You always did when it mattered.”

A fist struck the front door.

The wood bent inward.

Eli took the clock from her and examined its crooked face. “You kept it.”

“You made it.”

“We made it. You designed the escapement.”

“I would remember.”

“You keep saying that.”

Another blow shook the house. A crack opened across the door.

“What do they want?” Mara asked.

“The same thing everyone wants. More time.”

The broken clock began to tick.

Once.

Twice.

Its single hand moved from one to two.

“I never repaired it,” Mara whispered.

“You weren’t supposed to repair it. You were supposed to bring it back.”

Eli turned the clock around. A small brass keyhole waited in the rear panel. Mara inserted the key Tomas had given her.

It fit.

When she turned it, the clock sprang apart.

Gears unfolded like metal flowers. Slender arms extended from the wooden case. Rings of brass spun around a dark center in which stars appeared—tiny, cold, and impossibly distant.

The faceless people screamed.

The door shattered.

They entered in a pale crowd, filling the house shoulder to shoulder. Their unfinished faces tilted toward the clock.

Eli shouted something Mara could not hear. The bells overhead were ringing now, hundreds of them, each with a different voice. Some laughed. Some wept. Some called names.

The clock’s hand passed six.

A faceless woman caught Eli by the arm. He tore free, leaving a strip of yellow cloth in her fingers. Mara swung the lantern. Glass broke against the woman’s shoulder, and blue fire raced over her dress. She did not burn. Instead, a face flickered into being: old eyes, a child’s mouth, a nose made of shadow. Then it vanished.

“They’re memories,” Mara said.

“Possibilities,” Eli replied. “Lives that almost happened. Hours no one lived.”

The hand reached ten.

The red door appeared at the back of the house, standing open onto the dark stairway beneath the tower.

“Go!” Eli shouted.

Mara seized him. “Both of us.”

“I told you. The door needs a keeper.”

“Then they can keep it.”

“If no one does, this place floods into ours. Every lost moment returns at once. The dead come home. The unborn arrive. Yesterday sits beside tomorrow. The world stops.”

“Then we find another way.”

“We had eleven years to find another way.”

“No. I forgot. You waited.”

The hand reached twelve.

There was one number left.

Thirteen.

Eli looked exactly as he had on the last night: frightened, stubborn, young.

Mara understood then that waiting was not the same as living. He had spent eleven years in a single hour, preserving a town that mourned him and a sister who had forgotten her guilt.

She took his face between her hands.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’m not leaving you again.”

“Mara—”

“When the hand reaches thirteen, does the door close?”

“Yes.”

“And it needs a keeper?”

“Yes.”

“Not a prisoner?”

His eyes widened.

Mara pushed him toward the red door.

He struggled, but she had the strength of forty-three years and every morning she had risen without him. Every clock she had repaired, every winter she had endured, every silent meal had hardened something within her.

“No!” he shouted. “You can’t.”

“I’m older.”

“That’s not a reason.”

“I’ve had my time.”

“That’s not a reason either!”

The faceless crowd closed around them.

Mara pressed her forehead to his.

“Then let this be the reason: I am your sister, and this time you will obey me when it matters.”

She shoved him through the red door.

Eli landed on the stone steps beyond. He turned, but the crowd surged between them. His hand reached through a narrowing gap.

“Mara!”

“Ring the western bell!”

“The rope is cut!”

“You were always good at fixing things.”

“I made one clock!”

“And you put thirteen hours on it.”

The clock struck.

The sound was not loud. It was the delicate chime of a spoon touching a glass.

The faceless people stopped.

Outside, the summer sky cracked from horizon to horizon.

Behind Eli, deep in the real world, the tide began to return.

“You’ll forget me,” Mara said.

He shook his head fiercely.

“That is the price.”

“No.”

“It’s all right.”

“It isn’t.”

“No,” she agreed. “But it will have to be.”

The hand moved onto thirteen.

The red door slammed.

For one moment, Mara stood in complete silence.

Then the lost hour came apart.

Streets rose into the sky like ribbons. Houses folded flat. The faceless crowd burst into showers of rain, each drop containing an unlived life. Mara saw herself married to a fisherman she had once kissed at a midsummer dance. She saw Eli as an old man with silver hair. She saw their mother alive, opening her pantry to find every peppermint sweet untouched.

The visions passed through her and were gone.

The bells fell quiet.

Mara found herself alone beside the fountain.

The broken clock rested at her feet, ticking steadily. Its hand had returned to one.

She picked it up and walked toward the western tower, though no tower stood there now. Only a narrow house with a red door.

Inside, hundreds of bells waited overhead.

Mara sat at the table.

Beyond the windows, the lost town rebuilt itself beneath an unmoving summer sun. Faceless people wandered through the square. Somewhere far above, on the other side of the sea, morning approached.

At seven, Eli Vale woke on the wet stones beneath the western bell.

He was twenty-six years late and remembered nothing of where he had been.

The tide foamed around his boots. In his hand he held a brass key. Beside him stood an old lantern, a broken clock, and a sealed gray letter addressed in handwriting he did not recognize.

He opened it.

**Your sister is alive beneath the western bell.**

Eli read the sentence several times.

He had no sister.

At least, he could not remember one.

Yet grief rose in him, sudden and vast, and for a while he could do nothing but kneel in the shallow water and weep for someone whose face was gone.

When the tide climbed to his knees, the western bell rang above him.

Its rope had been cut eleven years before, but now a new one hung from the bronze mouth, braided from yellow cloth and strands of gray hair.

The first note rolled across Bellweather.

In the north tower, the keeper woke and pulled his rope. The southern bell answered, then the eastern, then the central. Lights appeared in windows. Doors opened. People stepped into the rain and looked toward the tower that had been silent for so long.

Eli rose.

Inside the bell’s fading voice, he heard the ticking of hundreds of clocks and a woman saying his name.

He climbed the tower stairs.

At the top, carved into the stone beneath the bell, he found instructions written in a narrow, slanting hand:

**RING AT DAWN.**

**RING AT STORM.**

**RING WHEN THE SEA BEGINS TO WRITE.**

Below that, in smaller letters:

**DO NOT LET ME BE FORGOTTEN.**

Eli traced the final words with his fingertips.

Then he took hold of the rope and rang the bell again.

Far beneath him, in the hour that gets lost, Mara heard it.

The faceless people paused in their wandering. The fixed sun shivered. One of the small bells above her table answered with a bright note.

Mara smiled.

Every morning after that, at seven, Eli found a letter on the tower steps.

Some contained warnings of storms. Some held names of sailors who could still be saved. Others offered instructions for repairing strange clocks that appeared overnight in his workshop, though he could not remember opening a workshop or learning the trade.

One letter simply said:

**You still sleep with one foot outside the blankets.**

Another:

**Peppermint was never safe around you.**

And another:

**When you were six, you believed the moon followed you home because it was lonely.**

Eli kept every letter.

Years passed. His hair silvered. Bellweather changed around him. New houses rose, old boats sank, children learned the story of the man who had returned from the sea without a past.

Each dawn he rang the western bell.

Each morning the letters came.

With them, memory returned—not all at once, and never completely, but in flashes. A girl laughing on a cliff path. Oil-stained fingers guiding his over a stubborn gear. A hand holding his in a storm.

At last, on a calm autumn morning, the sea left no letter.

Eli waited until noon.

At sunset, he unlocked the hidden door and descended with the thirteen-hour clock in his arms. He was an old man by then, but his steps were certain.

At the bottom, the red door stood open.

Beyond it, beneath a clear summer sky, a woman waited beside a fountain. She looked forty-three, exactly as she had when the lost hour claimed her.

This time, Eli remembered her face.

“You took your time,” Mara said.

He smiled, and the gap between his front teeth showed just as it had when he was fifteen.

“I was busy.”

Behind him, the red door swung shut.

Above the sea, the five bells began to ring, though no human hand pulled their ropes.
